Achraf El Abed est un homme hors du comm: Achraf El Abed is an extraordinary man and a talented professional dancer. With his old-school moustache, his jewellery and his dazzling smile, he embodies both North African tradition and the boldest modernity. He is a man who proudly represents Tunisia, heir to a history that is African, Arab, Amazigh, Muslim and Jewish.
Pourtant, il choque car c’est habillé co: And yet he shocks, because he dresses as a woman and, above all, dances Tunisian popular dance, the chaâbi tunsi, the way women do. And people from the Tunisian, North African and Middle Eastern diasporas turn out to see him at Montréal festivals, Arab nights and the city’s Tunisian restaurants.
Quand nous l’avons rencontré avec Aude S: When we met him, along with Aude Simon, the videographer who put together a beautiful video of our conversation that I invite you to watch, he welcomed us into his home. His apartment is a mix of Tunisian pottery, LGBTQIA+ flags, badges from every festival where he has performed, vintage photos of the women in his life, his mother and his grandmother, and above all an incredible collection of jewellery and traditional Tunisian women’s dance costumes.
Le contact a tout de suite été facile, t: We connected right away, because Achraf is such a welcoming, warm and open person. We talked about his life. We talked about stambeli, a spiritual dance that exists in my country, Morocco, under another name, gnawa, or diwane in Algeria. We talked about discrimination, social pressure, the concept of hchouma, so present in the Maghreb, even in diaspora families. We talked about love, freedom, art, exile.
Son parcours a été difficile mais illumi: His journey has been difficult but lit up by a great deal of optimism. I hope you will enjoy reading this profile as much as I enjoyed meeting Achraf. Because meeting Achraf means stepping into a world of joy, tradition and pride.
Avec sa moustache à l’ancienne, ses cein: With his old-school moustache, his belts of jingling bells and standing six feet tall, Achraf El Abed is a professional dancer of women’s popular dance in the Maghreb. In Tunisia, he is a celebrity who dances, yes, but the way women do. Enough to shock, or at the very least, surprise. Gay and an activist through his art, threatened with death in his country, he has been a refugee in Canada since 2022. Yet nothing pulls his heart away from Tunisia, which he loves above all else and hopes to return to one day.
« Je suis amazigh, africain, arabe, musu: “I’m Amazigh, African, Arab, Muslim, and I have a German Jewish grandfather… I represent Tunisia and all its blends. When I dance, it smells like back home,” Achraf El Abed says, laughing. “I recreate the Tunisian atmosphere, and that’s why people come to see me perform. And believe me, in Tunisia, we know how to party!” says the man who has dusted off a dance long reserved for the working classes and somewhat looked down upon for that very reason. Like Proust’s madeleine, he stirs the memories of Quebec’s Tunisian diaspora, as well as its Maghrebi and Middle Eastern communities.
<em>La Converse</em> l’a rencontré chez: La Converse met him at home, in his own world, with Oum Kalthoum playing in the background, to talk about his life, his artistic career and his activism. Smiling and welcoming, he proudly wears his rings, his earrings and holds a large fan on which is written “Love.”
C’est à l’âge de quatre ans que tout a c: It all began when Achraf El Abed was four years old. “I remember it like it was yesterday. At one of my cousins’ weddings, my mother surprised the newlyweds. She got up on stage in a wig and a belly dancer’s outfit, and she danced. Nobody recognized her, but I did. I remember her red dress embroidered with silver, I remember everything. I discovered dance that day. I was blown away. I’ve never stopped dancing since,” he recalls.
Achraf El Abed a grandi dans une famille: Achraf El Abed grew up in a close-knit family in the La Marsa neighbourhood of Tunis, surrounded by his mother, his aunts, and above all his beloved grandmother, the matriarch. “I was raised in a multigenerational home, and I discovered my feminine side through all these women who taught me freedom. The context wasn’t easy, because my mother, as a divorced woman at a time when there were few divorces, faced discrimination. I grew up drawing inspiration from her strength,” he says.
« Lorsque j’avais cinq ans, ma mère m’a: “When I was five, my mother tied a scarf around my hips at a birthday party and I danced like her. Everyone applauded me. I felt so happy, I was on stage for the first time,” he says with emotion. “Since then, I’ve danced with major Tunisian companies, on stages around the world. Yet I have never again reached that same joy.”
Pendant sa petite enfance, Achraf El Abe: In his early childhood, Achraf El Abed danced by imitating his mother, under the delighted gaze of his family. “And then one day, around the age of eight, I was told, stop dancing, it’s for women. It wasn’t the act of dancing I was being blamed for, because men dance in Tunisia, but the way I danced. As long as I was little, I was encouraged. Then it stopped, all of a sudden. The only question I asked myself was: why?” he continues. A total incomprehension for the child, suddenly plunged into a logic imposed by society. He kept dancing nonetheless, but only when he was alone and felt safe. And always with that feeling of shame, of hchouma, a Maghrebi word that refers to scandal but also to the modesty one is expected to show in society.
<strong>Le stambeli, la transe dansée hé: Stambeli, the trance dance inherited from enslaved people
C’est le stambeli, une danse spirituelle: It was stambeli, a Tunisian spiritual dance inherited from enslaved Black populations, that allowed him to dance in front of an audience again. “I grew up with this ancestral ritual of trance dance and music, thanks to my family, and especially my grandmother, who hosted stambeli gatherings at her home every year. It has always been part of my family,” explains Achraf El Abed. “This spiritual tradition is not gendered. At the age of twelve, I danced to call the spirits, as stambeli tradition has it, and I called the… feminine spirits. No matter how I danced, I was legitimate,” he shares.
Dans une société où le corps masculin do: In a society where the male body dominates, <l1>stambeli</l1> offers a space where the feminine divine and the masculine divine are equal. Men and women thus cross the boundary of gender, often through cross-dressing, to call upon spirits and saints. When he realizes he is gay, in adolescence, Achraf El Abed feels particularly at home in this community where the line between genders is blurred. “I didn’t need to announce my sexuality, I was part of this spiritual community and I was accepted for who I was.”
C’est à l’université qu’il prend réellem: It was at university that he truly took flight and discovered who he was. “At university I discovered what being gay meant. I also discovered culture, beauty, life. I set myself free.” To keep dancing, he joined a body performance club. Self-taught, and barely in the club, he was noticed for his talent. Although he had no experience, a professor suggested he perform in a show alongside a ballerina. “I had no experience. But she told me, ‘Yes, you are a professional dancer. You have something, trust yourself.’ That’s where it all began.”
Très vite, il danse avec les plus grands: Very quickly, he was dancing with Tunisia’s greatest performers. He blended his knowledge of stambeli with street jazz, contemporary… He observed, learned fast and performed by improvising. One of the masters of Tunisia’s national ballet, a founder of the country’s national dance company, took him under his wing. With his troupe, he was invited to dance all over the country and increasingly incorporated Tunisian popular dance. “For me, chaâbi tunsi is pure joy. Men have always danced, if only because for a long time women weren’t allowed to dance in the presence of men. Either the male dancers hid their masculine attributes under a veil, or they cross-dressed. I was lucky to be one of the last students of a cross-dressing dancer. For me, dance was liberating because I couldn’t openly say I was gay. I said it by dancing,” he says.
Petit à petit, il arrête le design et le: Little by little, he gave up design and applied arts, which he had graduated in and which paid his bills, to devote himself full time to this art form. Tunisian popular dance, long underestimated, grew in prominence, and Achraf El Abed was increasingly in demand for tours in Tunisia and abroad.
By day, he remained faithful to stambeli. But by night, he proudly donned the bells on his feet, his jewellery and his feminine silk-embroidered outfits, and danced the chaâbi. At the time, his family didn’t know he had gone from the sacred stambeli dance to the feminine chaâbi. “They found out by seeing me dance on television. My whole family told me it was shameful, hchouma. For my father, I had dirtied our family name. I haven’t seen my half-brothers on my father’s side in ten years. My mother tried to convince me to stop. How could I do this to her, a divorced woman already stigmatized… But I have no regrets. My legitimacy on stage gives me a sense of assurance in relation to my family. I don’t care what people think now. What do you mean, that I’m gay? Well, yes,” he says matter-of-factly.
<strong>Harcelé, insulté et adulé à la f: Harassed, insulted and adored all at once
Achraf El Abed devient célèbre en Tunisi: Achraf El Abed became famous in Tunisia. A popularity that nonetheless put him in danger: society stigmatizes and condemns homosexuality. It is also a crime punishable by three years in prison under Article 230 of the penal code, inherited from French colonization.
Harcelé, insulté et adulé à la fois, par: Harassed, insulted and adored all at once, sometimes by the same people, he no longer went out without earphones in his ears and sunglasses on. His brother lost his job several times because he was the brother of “the dancer.” “At first, I stayed impassive. Then, when it started to affect my family, I began to respond and defend myself, it really got to me. I was experiencing cyberharassment, street harassment. My mother was scared when she read the press and social media, she would tell me, ‘Achraf, they’re going to kill you.’ I received two serious death threats, and when I went to the police, the officer told me I just had to stop dancing. But dance is my whole life!” he says.
“I didn’t want to leave Tunisia. I love my country. I have never felt as much love as at home, despite the difficulties. When I learned that at every place where I performed, a man I didn’t know was looking for me, I understood that I was truly in danger. I opened my passport and checked which of my foreign visas was still valid. I had one for Canada, since I had been invited there for a series of performances. Without telling anyone, I left. At first, it was to escape this harassment, not necessarily to stay in Montréal. I was housed for two months by a Tunisian friend, also an activist, and I finally decided to stay and claim asylum. I love Montréal. I’m trying to build myself a ‘family’ here: dancers, people from the LGBTQIA+ community, immigrants, refugees…” says Achraf El Abed. “Obviously I feel even more at ease at the intersection of struggles, with Arab LGBTQIA+ people. With them, I don’t feel judged.”
Achraf El Abed continue de se produire a: Achraf El Abed continues to perform in Quebec: Festival Orientalys, Festival du Monde arabe, community days, Arab nights such as Laylit or Haram Party, artistic residencies… Since his arrival in April 2022, he has performed nearly three hundred times.
Pourtant, même à Montréal, les insultes: Yet even in Montréal, the insults continue. On top of the homophobic insults, the dancer also has to endure racist ones, notably on social media. “I am a Tunisian, Muslim man who dances a feminine dance. I don’t have to justify myself,” says the dancer, who continues to defend LGBTQIA+ rights as well as his art in panels and conferences. He also hopes to help change the image of North Africans, Arabs and Muslims. “Many people imagine us as violent, moustached machos living in our tents in the desert. I’m helping to change that image. I’m proud of who I am. I received a heritage. Yes, a heritage in a box, but I think outside that box.”
